title: Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
gist: A BMJ Case Reports paper describes a UK man in his 20s who survived a knife that passed through his right eye and his brain's left frontal and temporal lobes; surgeons used a conservative 'pull-and-see' extraction and he remained neurologically well, though he lost the eye. Doctors conclude outcome depends more on trajectory relative to critical structures than on apparent severity. No investable angle.

insights.claim: A UK man in his 20s arrived conscious with a 15 mm-wide knife blade through his right eye and brain, scoring 12 on the Glasgow Coma Scale.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Medical curiosity with no direct investment relevance.
insights.locator: A man in his 20s showed up

insights.claim: Surgeons removed part of the skull and used a conservative pull-and-see technique to slide the blade out, finding no significant hemorrhage; the eye was removed.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Illustrates conservative surgical approach for penetrating brain injuries.
insights.locator: After consulting with various medical specialties

insights.claim: The patient recovered rapidly, with transient right-side weakness resolving within two days, no infections or seizures, and preserved language and motor function.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.locator: The man then moved to intensive care

insights.claim: Doctors concluded outcomes of penetrating brain injuries may depend less on external severity than on the precise trajectory relative to critical vascular, cortical and subcortical structures.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Framework for clinical triage; marginal relevance to imaging and neurosurgery planning tools.
insights.quote: outcome may depend less on external severity than on precise trajectory relative to critical vascular, cortical and subcortical structures
